conventions.convention: Brownian filtrations are kept in four distinct layers after completing the ambient space: raw natural F0_t = sigma(B_s : 0 <= s <= t), raw right limit F0_{t+} = intersection over u > t of F0_u (the germ at 0), completed raw Fbar_t = sigma(F0_t union N) with N the subsets of ambient P-null sets, and usual augmentation F_t = intersection over u > t of Fbar_u; only F_t is asserted right-continuous, and N is a sigma-ideal.

On path space R^[0,infinity) the word Borel means measurable for the product sigma-algebra generated by finite coordinate cylinders; this is explicitly not the possibly larger Borel sigma-algebra of the uncountable product topology.

Null-path normalization: one fixed measurable probability-one event of continuity (and zero start) is chosen and the whole path is replaced by zero off it; indistinguishability means equality at every time on one such measurable full event, not modification; on a noncomplete space measurability of the entire all-times equality set is not asserted.

Quadratic variation is always taken along a named partition sequence with mesh tending to zero; partitions need not refine one another; the step and partial-increment partial sums are distinguished and the convergence mode (pointwise, uniform, uniform in probability) is part of every statement; a family indexed by positive integers is re-indexed to start at zero.

Quadratic covariation [X,Y] is declared to exist only when one common continuous-path limit arises uniformly in probability along every deterministic vanishing-mesh partition sequence and for both the step and partial-increment conventions; random, path-adapted or non-vanishing-mesh partitions are outside the convention.

Elementary Ito integrands are left-endpoint sums with coefficients measurable at the left endpoint (the coefficient is not asserted to equal H at the partition point), and the integral of a square-integrable predictable process is a (dt times P)-class defined by an L2 limit along any admissible elementary sequence; time integrals are truncations, integral of H over [0,t] = integral of H 1_[0,t].

Localization interface: the filtration satisfies the usual conditions, the energy process is A_t = integral of H squared over [0,t], local square-integrability means A_t < infinity almost surely for every finite t, canonical localization times are sigma_n = inf{t : A_t >= n}, tau_n = sigma_n and n, and all path functionals are normalized to zero off the common full continuity event.

Unbounded operators carry their domain as part of the data; S contained in T means containment of graphs; closedness is closedness of the graph in H direct-sum H; the resolvent is R_T(z) = (z - T)^{-1} with bounded everywhere-defined inverse required for z in the resolvent set.

PVM calculus conventions: inner product linear in the first variable; E_x(B) = inner product of E(B)x with x; E_{x,y} the polarized finite complex measure; D(f(E)) = {x : integral of |f|^2 dE_x < infinity}; f(E) is the norm limit of Phi_E(f restricted to |f| <= n); the zero Hilbert space is handled by a direct convention; Countable Choice for the bounded calculus and AC for the spectral construction.
Deficiency subspaces are K_+ = ker(T* - i) and K_- = ker(T* + i), and the von Neumann extension has domain D(T) direct-sum {u + Vu : u in K_+} with T_V(x + u + Vu) = Tx + iu - iVu.

The Brownian generator is L = one half Laplacian acting on C^2 functions (space-time version on the space variable only), with the coefficient convention that an Ito formula second-order term one half sum over i,j of (sigma sigma transpose)^{ij} partial_i partial_j equals L f exactly when sigma sigma transpose = I; no semigroup-domain or closed-operator claim is made.

Strong Markov measurable-version convention at random times: tau_n = 2^{-n} ceiling(2^n tau) on {tau < infinity} and infinity otherwise, and the shifted path is the finite limit of B at tau_n + u when it exists with tau < infinity, zero otherwise; on one measurable full event this agrees with the literal path values for all u.

load_bearing.statement: Standing hypothesis (H): B is adapted to (F_t) and for all 0 <= s < t the increment B_t - B_s is independent of F_s with law N(0, t - s). An elementary predictable Brownian integrand on [0,T] is a process H_s = sum over k from 0 to m-1 of xi_k times 1_(t_k,t_(k+1)] with 0 = t_0 < ... < t_m = T, each xi_k bounded and F_(t_k)-measurable; values at partition points are irrelevant.

After replacing the ambient space by its completion, four families are defined: raw natural F0_t = sigma(B_s : 0 <= s <= t); raw right limit F0_(t+) = intersection over u > t of F0_u (the germ at t = 0); completed raw Fbar_t = sigma(F0_t union N) with N the subsets of ambient P-null sets; and usual augmentation F_t = intersection over u > t of Fbar_u, which is increasing, right-continuous and contains N.

For an elementary integrand H_s = sum of xi_k 1_(t_k,t_(k+1)] with bounded F_(t_k)-measurable xi_k, the Ito integral is the process I_t(H) = sum over k of xi_k times (B at min(t,t_(k+1)) minus B at min(t,t_k)), 0 <= t <= T; the definition fixes adaptedness, linearity on a common refinement, and treats representation-dependence as temporary.

For a predictable H with E integral over [0,T] of H squared finite, the Ito integral is the L2(P) limit of elementary integrals along any bounded elementary sequence converging to H in L2(dt times P); the limit is independent of the sequence, and the integral over [0,t] is defined as the integral over [0,T] of H restricted to [0,t].

For predictable H, K with finite energy the integral is linear in H and K as an identity of L2(P) classes; the map H to the integral over [0,T] is an isometry with E(integral)^2 = E integral of H squared, takes mean-zero values, satisfies the cross identity E[(integral of H)(integral of K)] = E integral of H K, has closed image, and is injective modulo (dt times P)-classes.

Under the usual conditions, the energy process of a predictable H is A_t = integral over [0,t] of H squared, and H is locally square-integrable when A_t < infinity almost surely for every finite t. On G = intersection over m of {A_m < infinity} (a full event whose complement lies in F_0) the paths of A are finite and continuous, and the canonical times sigma_n = inf{t : A_t >= n}, tau_n = sigma_n and n satisfy tau_n increasing to infinity almost surely.

For a predictable H with finite energy on every [0,T] there is an adapted process M with continuous paths such that M_t equals the integral over [0,t] almost surely for every t, and M is a square-integrable martingale with E M_t squared equal to E integral of H squared over [0,t]; any two such versions are indistinguishable, equality meaning equality at every time on one measurable probability-one event.

For a locally square-integrable predictable H with canonical times tau_n there is an adapted process M = H dot B with continuous paths whose stopped pieces M^{tau_n} are indistinguishable from the finite-energy integrals of H 1_(0,tau_n]; M is unique up to indistinguishability among such continuous processes, independent of the localizing sequence, and satisfies E M_(t and tau_n) squared = E A_(t and tau_n) <= n; for finite-energy G and a stopping time sigma, (G dot B)_(t and sigma) = integral over [0,t] of G 1_(0,sigma].

For a continuous x on [0,T], a partition sequence is a sequence of partitions whose mesh tends to zero, with no refinement or regularity assumed. Two partial sums are attached: the step convention [x]^step_t = sum of squared increments up to the last partition point not exceeding t, and the partial-increment convention which adds the terminal squared increment; the convergence mode is part of every later statement, and the two conventions differ by at most the squared maximal oscillation.

For real processes with almost-sure continuous paths, the quadratic covariation [X,Y] exists on [0,T] when there is a continuous-path process such that for every deterministic partition sequence of [0,T] with mesh tending to zero both the step and partial-increment cross-increment partial sums converge to it uniformly in probability; the same process must arise for every admissible sequence and for both conventions.

A real progressively measurable X is a continuous Brownian Ito process when there are a finite F_0-measurable X_0, a progressively measurable drift b with locally finite absolute integral, and a predictable locally square-integrable sigma such that X_t = X_0 + integral of b + localized Ito integral of sigma, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event; a vector version driven by m-dimensional Brownian motion is defined componentwise.

For a real continuous Brownian Ito process X and f in C^{1,2}([0,infinity) times R), up to indistinguishability for every t >= 0, f(t,X_t) = f(0,X_0) + integral over [0,t] of (partial_t f + b partial_x f + one half sigma squared partial_x^2 f)(s,X_s) ds + localized Ito integral of sigma_s partial_x f(s,X_s), with the integrands read through the stated normalization convention.

Let B be standard Brownian motion with usual augmentation and let tau be a stopping time finite almost surely. Then B_tau is F_tau-measurable, the increment process (B_(tau+t) - B_tau) is independent of F_tau with Wiener finite-dimensional marginals, and for every bounded Borel functional Phi on the product sigma-algebra of R^[0,infinity), E[Phi of the shifted path given F_tau] = Psi_Phi(B_tau) almost surely, where Psi_Phi(x) is the Wiener integral of Phi(x + w).

For a self-adjoint operator T on a nonzero complex Hilbert space there is a unique regular projection valued measure E on the Borel sigma-algebra of R such that D(T) = {x : integral of lambda squared dE_x(lambda) < infinity} and Tx = integral of lambda dE(lambda)x on D(T); conversely, for any regular PVM E on R the operator given by that integral with that domain is self-adjoint and has E as its spectral PVM.

For a self-adjoint T with spectral PVM E and Borel f, g on R: f(T)* = conjugate f (T); f(T)g(T) has domain D(g(T)) intersect D((fg)(T)) and equals the restriction of (fg)(T), with closure (fg)(T); on D(f(T)) intersect D(g(T)) the sum agrees with (f+g)(T) and its closure is (f+g)(T); the spectrum of f(T) is the E-essential range of f, which for continuous f is the closure of f(sigma(T)).

For a standard Brownian motion with usual augmented natural filtration: (1) for every T > 0 and every Z in L2(F_T) there is a predictable H with finite energy on [0,T] such that Z = EZ + integral over [0,T] of H dB almost surely, the conditional expectation martingale agrees with the continuous integral up to indistinguishability, and H is unique modulo (dt times P)-null sets; (2) every local martingale with cadlag paths on one full event equals M_0 + integral of a locally square-integrable predictable H up to indistinguishability, hence has a continuous version.

concerns.concern: Step 1.1 extends the spectral PVM F_0 of the Cayley transform C from sigma(C) to the unit circle by F(B) := F_0(B intersect sigma(C)) and asserts that F is a regular PVM on the circle; the regularity of B to F_0(B intersect sigma(C)) is not argued at that point, and the item's own regularity-transfer fact [A5] covers only the homeomorphism transport used later in step 3.1. The intended justification is immediate (for each x the scalar measure F_x is the pushforward of the regular Borel measure (F_0)_x under the inclusion of the compact set sigma(C) into the circle), but step 5.2 applies the support/uniqueness theorem to F on the circle, so the assertion is used.

seams_checked.note: Opened the six cited group-c items and compared them with every citing passage in the unbounded page. def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm and lem-unbounded-pvm-integral-is-well-defined-and-closed use the PVM definition (self-adjoint idempotent values, E(B intersect C) = E(B)E(C), strong countable additivity, contractivity), the scalar-measure lemma (E_x positive of mass norm(x)^2, E_{x,y} finite complex with |E_{x,y}|(X) at most norm(x)norm(y)), the bounded integral (unique operator with the pairing identity, norm bound, quadratic identity) and the star-homomorphism theorem (linearity, unitality, multiplicativity, conjugation, strong limits), and both items flag the nonzero-Hilbert-space hypothesis and supply Countable Choice explicitly. thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators cites the bounded normal spectral theorem for existence and uniqueness of the regular spectral PVM and the support/uniqueness theorem for support equal to the spectrum and uniqueness on compact sets, matching both statements without weakening hypotheses or changing direction. thm-kato-rellich, thm-canonical-spectral-type-decomposition, def-discrete-and-essential-spectrum-of-a-self-adjoint-operator, thm-weyl-criterion-for-essential-spectrum, thm-continuous-functional-calculus-under-resolvent-convergence, cor-unitary-groups-converge-under-strong-resolvent-convergence, lem-spectral-form-domain-and-core-of-a-semibounded-operator, def-relative-compactness-with-respect-to-an-operator and thm-min-max-principle-below-essential-spectrum cite only the PVM definition and the bounded PVM calculus under their stated hypotheses, with the zero-space case handled either explicitly or by the zero-space convention. No reverse citations from the spectral page items to the unbounded page; no domain, quantifier, hypothesis, direction or conclusion was changed in any citing passage.
